props.title: The Show Must Go On

sections.content: **The Show Must Go On (2007)** (2007) stands as a powerful entry in Korean crime cinema, directed by Han Jae-rim with Song Kang-ho delivering a masterful performance as In-gu, a middle-aged gangster trying to go straight. The film brilliantly subverts expectations of the crime genre, much like A Bittersweet Life (2005) and New World (2013), by focusing on the mundane struggles of a criminal rather than glorifying violence. Song Kang-ho, who also stunned in **Memories of Murder** (2003) and **Parasite** (2019), brings remarkable depth to In-gu's character as he attempts to balance his criminal past with his desire for a normal family life.

sections.content: The film's exploration of family dynamics within criminal contexts recalls other Korean crime masterpieces like **The Chaser** (2008) and Mother (2009). Director Han Jae-rim crafts tense domestic scenes that carry as much weight as the violent confrontations, creating a unique hybrid of family drama and crime thriller. The film's visual style employs a muted color palette and naturalistic lighting that grounds the story in reality, contrasting sharply with the more stylized approach of contemporaries like The Man from Nowhere (2010).

What sets **The Show Must Go On** (2007) apart is its unflinching look at the toll of criminal life on family relationships. Unlike the glamorized portrayals in films like **Goodfellas** (1990) or **The Godfather** (1972), Han Jae-rim focuses on the grinding daily pressure of maintaining a facade of normalcy. The protagonist's struggle mirrors similar themes in **A Dirty Carnival** (2006), where the criminal lifestyle inevitably corrupts attempts at legitimate existence. sections.content: **The Show Must Go On** (2007) represents a crucial transition point in Korean crime cinema, bridging the gap between the ultra-violent revenge films of the early 2000s like **Oldboy** (2003) and the more nuanced character studies that would follow, such as **The Yellow Sea** (2010). The film's influence can be seen in later works like **The Gangster, The Cop, The Devil** (2019), which similarly examine the human cost of criminal life while maintaining genre tensions.
